fontes.trecho: Baker aided the French Resistance during World War II and also worked with the British Secret Intelligence Service and the United States Office of Strategic Services, to an extent which was not publicized until 2020, when French documents were declassified. [...] On November 30, 2021, Baker was inducted into the Panthéon in Paris, the first black woman to receive one of the highest honors in France. [...] In September 1939, when France declared war on Germany in response to the invasion of Poland, Baker was recruited by the Deuxième Bureau, the French military intelligence agency, as an "honorable correspondent". She worked with Jacques Abtey, the head of French counterintelligence in Paris. She socialized with the Germans at embassies, ministries, night clubs, charming them while secretly gathering information. Her café-society fame enabled her to rub shoulders with those in the know, from high-ranking Japanese officials to Italian and Vichy bureaucrats, reporting to Abtey what she heard. [...] Confident in her celebrity status and the protections it afforded, Baker believed she could operate without raising suspicion. To covertly transport sensitive information, she used methods such as writing notes on her hands and arms, pinning them inside her clothing, and using invisible ink. [...] she would shelter resistance fighters and Jewish refugees [...] As an entertainer, Baker had an excuse for moving around Europe, visiting neutral nations such as Portugal, as well as some in South America. She carried information for transmission to England, about airfields, harbors, and German troop concentrations [...] She pinned notes with the information she gathered inside her underwear. [...] When the Germans invaded France in 1940, Baker left Paris and went to the Château des Milandes, her home in the Dordogne [...] Notes were written in invisible ink on Baker's sheet music.

gancho: Para tirar do Irã seis diplomatas americanos escondidos, em 1980, a CIA abriu em Hollywood uma produtora de fachada, com telefonistas e anúncios em revistas, para um filme de ficção científica que jamais seria rodado.
explicacao: Quando estudantes islamistas tomaram a embaixada dos EUA em Teerã, em 4 de novembro de 1979, seis diplomatas escaparam e acabaram escondidos por diplomatas canadenses, entre eles o embaixador Ken Taylor. Para tirá-los do país, o oficial da CIA Tony Mendez, especialista em disfarces, propôs que eles se passassem por uma equipe de cinema procurando locações. Com ajuda do maquiador de Hollywood John Chambers, a CIA montou a "Studio Six Productions" num estúdio em Sunset Boulevard, com gente atendendo o telefone caso alguém ligasse para conferir, festa numa boate e anúncios nas revistas Variety e The Hollywood Reporter. O projeto de filme era real: uma adaptação abandonada do romance Lord of Light, de Roger Zelazny, que já tinha roteiro e arte conceitual de Jack Kirby. Mendez o rebatizou de Argo. O Canadá, por uma ordem secreta, deu aos seis passaportes canadenses autênticos. Houve um susto: os vistos tinham sido datados sem levar em conta o calendário iraniano, e um funcionário da embaixada percebeu o erro a tempo. Em 27 de janeiro de 1980, o grupo embarcou num voo da Swissair para Zurique. Para proteger os reféns que continuavam em Teerã, os dois governos esconderam o papel da CIA, revelado só em 1997. A operação inspirou, com muitas liberdades, o filme Argo, de 2012.

fontes.trecho: six American diplomats who had evaded capture during the seizure of the United States embassy in Tehran, Iran, on November 4, 1979, after the Iranian Revolution, when Islamist students took most of the American embassy personnel hostage [...] The "caper" involved two CIA officers (Tony Mendez and his colleague Ed Johnson) joining the six diplomats in Tehran to form a fake film crew. [...] On the morning of Sunday, January 27, 1980, the full eight-person party passed through passport control at Mehrabad Airport in Tehran, boarded a Swissair flight to Zürich [...] There they were greeted by Sheardown and Canadian Ambassador Ken Taylor, who agreed to host the Staffords at his own home [...] The CIA enlisted two disguise and exfiltration experts, Tony Mendez and Ed Johnson [...] Clark oversaw a secret Order-in-Council to grant the six an exemption to the passport law. [...] Mendez put together an audacious cover story: the six refugees would pose as members of a Hollywood crew scouting movie locations. [...] Mendez and Johnson enlisted the help of John Chambers, a veteran Hollywood make-up artist. They established a functioning office at Sunset Gower Studios on Sunset Boulevard, named "Studio Six Productions" (a nod to the six diplomats). [...] Telephones to the "Studio Six" office in Los Angeles were manned by staffers, in the event that anyone called to check the company's legitimacy. [...] He selected a stalled production of a film called Lord of Light, based on the 1967 Roger Zelazny science fiction novel of the same name [...] Jack Kirby had created concept art, and a script had been completed. But the project had been abandoned in November 1979, before the start of filming. Mendez renamed the film Argo [...] held a film party at a nightclub in Los Angeles, and took out early advertisements for the film in Variety and The Hollywood Reporter industry magazines. [...] A mistake had been made in dating the visas, as the Iranian year begins at the spring equinox, and the date of issue was actually well in the future. One of the Canadian embassy officers spotted the mistake while checking the documents. [...] The Argo story was blown, but both the Canadian and U.S. governments concealed the CIA's role in order to avoid retribution against the remaining American hostages by their captors. The CIA's full involvement was not revealed until 1997, when the agency declassified the records. [...] The article was used loosely—alongside a memoir Mendez wrote—by Chris Terrio as the basis of the 2012 film Argo.

gancho: Mata Hari foi fuzilada em 1917 acusada de causar a morte de 50 mil soldados. Para vários historiadores, foi um bode expiatório, e as mensagens que a denunciaram usavam um código que os alemães sabiam estar quebrado.
explicacao: Margaretha Zelle era holandesa e fez sucesso em Paris como uma dançarina exótica que dizia vir de Java; o próprio investigador do caso concluiu que boa parte da persona era inventada. Cidadã de um país neutro, ela cruzava fronteiras livremente durante a Primeira Guerra, o que chamava atenção. O serviço secreto francês chegou a lhe oferecer um milhão de francos para seduzir o príncipe herdeiro alemão. Em Madri, ela procurou o adido militar alemão e, ao que parece, ofereceu segredos franceses em troca de dinheiro. Em janeiro de 1917, esse adido mandou a Berlim mensagens de rádio sobre um espião de codinome H-21, com biografia tão parecida com a dela que a identificação era óbvia. Os franceses as interceptaram, mas o código era um que os alemães sabiam já ter sido quebrado, o que sugere uma armadilha para entregá-la, montada pelos próprios alemães, insatisfeitos com as fofocas que ela lhes vendia. Nem a França nem a Grã-Bretanha tinham prova definitiva contra ela. Só que a França vivia motins no exército e exaustão de guerra, e uma espiã alemã para culpar era conveniente; a imprensa exagerou muito sua importância. Ela nunca confessou e foi executada em Vincennes em 15 de outubro de 1917, aos 41 anos. Os autos, 1.275 páginas, só foram liberados pelo Exército francês em 2017.

fontes.trecho: was a Dutch exotic dancer and courtesan who was convicted of being a spy for Germany during World War I. She was executed by firing squad in France. [...] Later biographers argue that she was convicted and condemned because the French Army needed a scapegoat, and that the files used to secure her conviction contained falsifications. [...] During World War I, the Netherlands remained neutral. As a Dutch subject, Zelle was thus able to cross national borders freely. [...] her movements inevitably attracted attention. [...] the Deuxième Bureau offered Zelle one million francs if she could seduce him and provide France with good intelligence about German plans. [...] In late 1916, Zelle traveled to Madrid, where she met the German military attaché Major Arnold Kalle [...] Zelle apparently offered to share French secrets with the German Empire in exchange for money [...] In January 1917, Kalle transmitted radio messages to Berlin describing the helpful activities of a German spy code-named H-21, whose biography so closely matched Zelle's that it was obvious they were one and the same. [...] The messages were in a code that German intelligence knew had already been broken by the French, suggesting that the messages were contrived to have Zelle arrested by the French. [...] accused of spying for Germany and consequently causing the deaths of at least 50,000 soldiers. Although the French and British intelligence services suspected her of spying for Germany, neither could produce definite evidence against her. [...] Bouchardon established that much of the Mata Hari persona was invented. [...] The country was close to collapsing from war exhaustion. Having one German spy to blame for everything that went wrong with the war was convenient for the French government, and Mata Hari seemed the perfect scapegoat. The case against her received maximum publicity in the French press and led to her importance being greatly exaggerated. [...] Mata Hari actually made no such confession. [...] Zelle was executed in the moat of the Château de Vincennes, by a firing squad consisting of 12 French soldiers just before dawn on 15 October 1917. She was 41. [...] Mata Hari's sealed trial and other related documents, a total of 1,275 pages, were declassified by the French Army in 2017 [...] General Walter Nicolai, the chief intelligence officer of the German Imperial Army, had grown annoyed that Mata Hari had provided no real intelligence, instead selling the Germans mere Paris gossip [...] and decided to terminate her employment by exposing her as a German spy to the French.

gancho: Em 1943, os britânicos soltaram no mar da Espanha o corpo de um sem-teto vestido de oficial, com cartas falsas sobre invadir a Grécia e a Sardenha. Hitler acreditou e mandou reforços para lá. O alvo real era a Sicília.
explicacao: A Operação Mincemeat se inspirou num memorando de 1939 do chefe da inteligência naval britânica e de seu assistente, Ian Fleming, o futuro autor de James Bond. Os oficiais Ewen Montagu e Charles Cholmondeley conseguiram o corpo de Glyndwr Michael, um andarilho que morreu ao comer veneno de rato, e inventaram para ele uma vida inteira: Major William Martin, dos Royal Marines. Nos bolsos, a foto de uma noiva fictícia, Pam (na verdade, uma funcionária do MI5), duas cartas de amor dela e o recibo de um anel de noivado. Numa pasta, uma carta pessoal de um general britânico que citava a Sicília só como alvo de despiste. Um submarino deixou o corpo perto de Huelva, e um pescador o encontrou. A Espanha, oficialmente neutra, colaborava com a inteligência alemã. Em maio, Bletchley Park decifrou uma mensagem alemã que confirmava o sucesso, e Churchill recebeu o aviso: o Mincemeat fora engolido com anzol, linha e chumbada. Hitler ordenou defender a Grécia e a Sardenha a todo custo e transferiu uma divisão blindada da França para a Grécia. Quatro horas depois de começar a invasão da Sicília, em julho, aviões alemães ainda deixavam a ilha para reforçar a Sardenha. A identidade do morto só foi descoberta em 1996, por um historiador amador.

fontes.trecho: Operation Mincemeat was a successful British deception operation of the Second World War to disguise the 1943 Allied invasion of Sicily. Two members of British intelligence obtained the body of Glyndwr Michael, a tramp who died from eating rat poison, dressed him as an officer of the Royal Marines and placed personal items on him identifying him as the fictitious Captain (Acting Major) William Martin. Correspondence between two British generals that suggested that the Allies planned to invade Greece and Sardinia, with Sicily as merely the target of a diversionary attack, was also placed on [...] Mincemeat was based on the 1939 Trout memo, written by Rear Admiral John Godfrey, the director of the Naval Intelligence Division, and his personal assistant, Lieutenant Commander Ian Fleming. [...] the body was transported to the southern coast of Spain by submarine and releasing it close to shore, where it was picked up the following morning by a Spanish fisherman. [...] whose nominally neutral government was known to co-operate with the Abwehr, the German military intelligence organisation. [...] These included a photograph of an invented fiancée named Pam; the image was of an MI5 clerk, Jean Leslie. Two love letters from Pam were included in the pocket litter, as was a receipt for a diamond engagement ring [...] Montagu and Cholmondeley [...] rejected those in favour of Huelva on the coast of southern Spain [...] Final proof that the Germans had been passed the information from the letters came on 14 May when a German communication was decrypted by the Ultra source of signals intelligence produced by the Government Code and Cypher School (GC&CS) at Bletchley Park. [...] to Churchill, then in the United States. It read "Mincemeat swallowed rod, line and sinker [...] Hitler informed Mussolini that Greece, Sardinia and Corsica must be defended "at all costs", and that German troops would be best placed to do the job. He ordered that the experienced 1st Panzer Division be transferred from France to Salonika, Greece. [...] On 9 July the Allies invaded Sicily in Operation Husky. German signals intercepted by GC&CS showed that even four hours after the invasion of Sicily began, twenty-one aircraft left Sicily to reinforce Sardinia. [...] In 1996 Roger Morgan, an amateur historian from London, uncovered evidence in the Public Record Office that the identity of the corpse was Michael.
Ann Fleming (widow of James Bond author Ian Fleming)

gancho: A rede de espiões de George Washington era tão secreta que nem ele sabia o nome de todos. Um líder só foi identificado por volta de 1930, quando um historiador comparou a letra de cartas de família com a dos relatórios.
explicacao: A rede Culper foi organizada em 1778 pelo major Benjamin Tallmadge e por Washington, durante a ocupação britânica de Nova York. O general tinha aprendido com o caso de Nathan Hale, capitão mandado como espião com identidade falsa, logo capturado e executado em 1776, e passou a preferir civis, que chamavam menos atenção. Os líderes usavam os codinomes Samuel Culper pai (Abraham Woodhull) e Samuel Culper filho (Robert Townsend). Townsend tinha negócios em Nova York, inclusive de alfaiataria, que lhe davam acesso a oficiais britânicos, e escrevia uma coluna social num jornal legalista cujo dono também era membro secreto da rede. As mensagens usavam um livro de códigos com números para palavras, pessoas e lugares, além de tinta invisível entre as linhas de cartas comuns. Townsend exigiu que Woodhull nunca revelasse seu nome a ninguém, nem a Washington. O público só soube da rede nos anos 1930. Por volta de 1930 (as fontes variam entre 1929 e 1930), o historiador Morton Pennypacker notou que a letra de cartas antigas da casa da família Townsend era parecida com a do "Culper Jr." nos papéis de Washington, e um perito em documentos confirmou a correspondência.

fontes.trecho: The Culper Ring was a network of spies active during the American Revolutionary War, organized by Major Benjamin Tallmadge and General George Washington in 1778 during the British occupation of New York City. [...] The leaders of the spy ring were Abraham Woodhull and Robert Townsend, using the aliases of "Samuel Culper Sr." and "Samuel Culper Jr.", respectively [...] Captain Nathan Hale, who went to New York City under a false identity but was quickly captured by the British and executed on September 22, 1776. [...] He decided that civilians would attract less attention than soldiers [...] Townsend was involved in business there, and his presence would arouse less suspicion than Woodhull's visits. He had access to British officers through several channels, including his own tailoring business. He also wrote a society column in a Loyalist newspaper and owned an interest in a coffeehouse with the newspaper's owner, James Rivington, who was also a secret member of the Culper Ring. [...] Secrecy was so strict that Washington did not know the identity of all of the operatives. [...] invisible ink, called a sympathetic stain, to write between the lines of what appeared to be typical letters. [...] he had completed pocket dictionaries with lists of verbs, nouns, people, and places with their corresponding code numbers. [...] The general public was unaware of the Culper Ring's existence until the 1930s. Robert Townsend's identity as "Culper Jr." was discovered in 1929 upon examination of old letters written by Townsend in the Townsend family home. The historian Morton Pennypacker reviewed the letters and noticed that the handwriting in letters from the trunk, written by Robert Townsend, was similar to the handwriting in letters written by "Samuel Culper Jr.", in Washington's collection. Pennypacker would then approach Questioned Document Examiner, Albert S. Osborn, to confirm the handwriting was a match.

He is one of the least-known operatives in the spy ring and once demanded that Abraham Woodhull ("Samuel Culper") never tell his name to anyone, even Washington. [...] The identity of Samuel Culper, Jr. was discovered only in 1930 by the New York historian Morton Pennypacker.

gancho: Na Segunda Guerra, a equipe de Elizebeth Friedman, da Guarda Costeira dos EUA, quebrou máquinas Enigma de uma rede de espiões nazistas na América do Sul. No fim da guerra, o FBI de Hoover alardeou a vitória sem citá-la.
explicacao: Friedman chegou às cifras por um caminho curioso: em 1916, foi contratada pelos Laboratórios Riverbank, de um rico comerciante, para ajudar uma pesquisadora que tentava provar que Francis Bacon escrevera as peças de Shakespeare. Lá conheceu o marido, William Friedman, e os dois viraram dos poucos especialistas em criptografia do país. Na Lei Seca, ela decifrou à mão mais de 12 mil mensagens de contrabandistas em três anos, o que levou a 650 processos. Na Segunda Guerra, sua unidade, então sob a Marinha, foi a principal fonte de inteligência americana sobre a rede clandestina alemã na América do Sul. A equipe resolveu vários sistemas de cifra, entre eles três máquinas Enigma, mais ou menos ao mesmo tempo que Bletchley Park, trabalhando de forma independente. Duas eram usadas pelo agente da SS que chefiava a operação. Mas J. Edgar Hoover lançou uma campanha dizendo que o FBI havia liderado a quebra dos códigos, com reportagem de revista e filme de propaganda que não mencionavam nem Friedman nem a Guarda Costeira. Ela tinha jurado à Marinha guardar segredo sobre seu papel até a morte, e cumpriu. Os documentos só foram liberados em 2008.

fontes.trecho: Elizebeth Smith began working at Riverbank Laboratories in Geneva, Illinois, in 1916. [...] Colonel George Fabyan, a wealthy textile merchant, owned Riverbank Laboratories and was interested in Shakespeare. [...] He told her that she would assist a Boston woman, Elizabeth Wells Gallup, and her sister with Gallup's attempt to prove Sir Francis Bacon had written Shakespeare's plays [...] On the staff at Riverbank was the man Elizebeth would marry in May 1917, William F. Friedman [...] there were only three or four people in the United States who knew anything about the subject. Two of those people were Elizebeth and William Friedman. [...] Friedman solved over 12,000 coded messages by hand in three years, resulting in 650 criminal prosecutions. [...] During World War II, Friedman's Coast Guard unit was transferred to the Navy, where they were the principal U.S. source of intelligence on Operation Bolívar, the clandestine German network in South America. [...] they solved numerous cipher systems used by the Germans and their local sympathizers, including three separate Enigma machines. [...] The two sections worked independently and ended up solving the machines around the same time. One turned out to be an unrelated Swiss network, but the other two were used by Johannes Siegfried Becker [...] the SS agent who headed the operation, to communicate with Germany. [...] At the end of World War II, Hoover began a public media campaign claiming that the FBI led the code-breaking effort that resulted in the collapse and arrest of the German spy network in South America. This effort included a story in The American Magazine titled "How the Nazi Spy Invasion Was Smashed" and a publicity film called The Battle of the United States. Neither mentioned Friedman or the Coast Guard. [...] Friedman had signed an oath with the U.S. Navy promising to keep her role in World War II secret until her death, and she did so. It was not until 2008 that the documents were finally declassified.

gancho: Os primeiros satélites espiões dos EUA soltavam o filme numa cápsula de paraquedas, que um avião apanhava no ar. Em 1960, uma só cápsula trouxe mais imagens da URSS que todos os voos anteriores do avião espião U-2.
explicacao: O programa Corona, da Força Aérea e da CIA, nasceu depois do choque do Sputnik e foi acelerado quando os soviéticos derrubaram um U-2, em maio de 1960. Para disfarçar, os lançamentos eram apresentados como "Discoverer", um programa científico cujas cápsulas trariam amostras biológicas; algumas foram até construídas para levar um macaco. O começo teve uma série de fracassos, e a cápsula do Discoverer 2 caiu perto de Spitsbergen e nunca foi achada. Em agosto de 1960, o Discoverer 13 fez a primeira recuperação de um objeto vindo da órbita, e dias depois o filme do Discoverer 14 foi apanhado no ar, sobre o Pacífico, por um avião de transporte C-119. Na volta, a cápsula descartava o escudo térmico a 18 km de altura e abria os paraquedas, e o avião a fisgava com uma garra rebocada. Se caísse no mar e ninguém a recolhesse, um tampão de sal se dissolvia em dois dias e a afundava. O impacto foi enorme: seis meses antes, uma estimativa da CIA previa de 140 a 200 mísseis intercontinentais soviéticos em 1961; em setembro de 1961, depois de mais um ano de fotos do Corona e de outras fontes, a estimativa oficial caiu para 10 a 25. O programa foi ultrassecreto até 1992, e as fotos foram liberadas em 1995.

fontes.trecho: prompted President Dwight D. Eisenhower to authorize the Corona program, a top-priority reconnaissance program managed by the Air Force and CIA. [...] The CORONA project was pushed forward rapidly after the Soviets shot down a U-2 on 1 May 1960. [...] the first CORONA satellites were cloaked with disinformation as being part of a space technology development program called Discoverer. To the public, Discoverer missions were scientific and engineering missions, the film-return capsules being used to return biological specimens. To facilitate this deception, several CORONA capsules were built to house a monkey passenger. [...] Recovery of the capsule was done in mid-air by a specially equipped aircraft. [...] The main bus performed well, but the capsule recovery failed, the SRV coming down over Spitzbergen rather than Hawaii. The capsule was never found. [...] There were four more partially successful and unsuccessful missions in the KH-1 series before Discoverer 13 (10 August 1960), which managed a fully successful capsule recovery for the first time. This was the first recovery of a man-made object from orbit [...] Two days after the 18 August 1960 launch of Discoverer 14, its film bucket was successfully retrieved in the Pacific Ocean by a Fairchild C-119 Flying Boxcar transport plane. [...] With the success of Discoverer 14, which returned 16 lb (7.3 kg) of film and provided more coverage of the Soviet Union than all preceding U2 flights [...] Six months before Discoverer 14, an NIE predicted that the Soviets would have 140–200 ICBMs deployed by 1961. [...] the heat shield surrounding the vehicle was jettisoned at 60,000 ft (18 km) and parachutes deployed. The capsule was intended to be caught in mid-air by a passing airplane towing an airborne claw which would then winch it aboard, or it could land at sea. A salt plug in the base would dissolve after two days, allowing the capsule to sink if it was not picked up by the United States Navy. [...] The CORONA program was officially classified top secret until 1992. On 22 February 1995, the photos taken by the CORONA satellites [...] were declassified

fontes.titulo: National Intelligence Estimate 11-8/1-61, 21 de setembro de 1961 (Foreign Relations of the United States, 1961–1963, vol. VIII)
fontes.trecho: Washington, September 21, 1961. [...] We now estimate that the present Soviet ICBM strength is in the range of 10-25 launchers

gancho: Autora de contos infantis budistas, criada na não violência de Gandhi, Noor Inayat Khan foi a primeira mulher que os britânicos mandaram à França ocupada como operadora de rádio. Presa, não entregou nenhuma informação.
explicacao: Noor nasceu em Moscou em 1914, filha de uma americana e de um músico indiano, mestre sufi, descendente de Tipu Sultan, governante de Mysore. Cresceu perto de Paris, estudou psicologia infantil na Sorbonne e música no conservatório, e em 1939 publicou um livro de contos inspirados nas histórias Jataka, da tradição budista. Com a guerra, ela e o irmão decidiram ajudar a derrotar o nazismo, mas sem matar ninguém. Ela entrou para a força aérea feminina, onde aprendeu radiotelegrafia, e depois para o SOE, o serviço secreto britânico de operações. Em junho de 1943, desembarcou na França. Operador de rádio era talvez o posto mais perigoso, porque os transmissores podiam ser rastreados. A rede a que ela servia começou a cair poucos dias depois, e ela preferiu ficar, pois acreditava ser a única operadora restante em Paris. Traída, foi presa em outubro e tentou fugir duas vezes. O chefe do serviço de segurança alemão em Paris testemunhou depois da guerra que ela não deu informação alguma e mentiu o tempo todo. Mas, contra as regras, Noor tinha copiado em cadernos as mensagens que enviara, e os alemães os usaram para se passar por ela. Foi executada em Dachau em 1944 e recebeu, depois de morta, a Cruz de George.

fontes.trecho: As an SOE agent under the codename Madeleine she became the first female wireless operator to be sent from the UK into occupied France to aid the French Resistance during the Second World War. Inayat Khan was betrayed, captured, and executed at Dachau concentration camp. She was posthumously awarded the George Cross for her service [...] Noor Inayat Khan was born on 1 January 1914, in Moscow. [...] Inayat Khan's great-great-grandfather was Tipu Sultan, the ruler of Mysore. Inayat Khan lived in Europe as a musician and a teacher of Sufism. Her mother, Pirani Ameena Begum (born Ora Ray Baker), was an American [...] She studied child psychology at the Sorbonne, and also music at the Paris Conservatory [...] In 1939, her book Twenty Jataka Tales, inspired by the Jataka tales of Buddhist tradition, was published in London [...] Although Noor was deeply influenced by pacifist ideals, she and her brother Vilayat decided they wanted to help defeat Nazi tyranny [...] In November 1940, Noor joined the Women's Auxiliary Air Force (WAAF) and, as an Aircraftwoman 2nd Class, was sent to be trained as a wireless operator. [...] probably the most dangerous work of all. [...] but the operators were highly vulnerable to detection [...] "You see, Nora and I had been brought up with the policy of Gandhi's nonviolence [...] "She said, 'Well, I must do something, but I don't want to kill anyone.' [...] From 24 June 1943 the 'Prosper' network that Noor had been sent to be a radio operator for began to be rounded up by the Germans. [...] When Buckmaster told her she would be flown home, she told him she would prefer to remain, as she believed she was the only radio operator remaining in Paris. [...] On or around 13 October 1943, Noor was arrested and interrogated at the SD Headquarters at 84 Avenue Foch in Paris. During that time, she attempted escape twice. Hans Kieffer, the former head of the SD in Paris, testified after the war that she did not give the Gestapo a single piece of information, but lied consistently. [...] Contrary to security regulations, Noor had copied out all the messages she had sent as an SOE operative [...] the Germans gained enough information from them to continue sending false messages imitating her. [...] On 12 September 1944, Noor Inayat Khan was abruptly transferred to the Dachau concentration camp [...] On 16/17 June 1943 [...] Noor was flown to landing ground B/20A 'Indigestion' in Northern France

gancho: O guardião dos quadros da rainha Elizabeth II, um dos maiores historiadores da arte do Reino Unido, confessou em 1964 que espionava para a URSS. Ganhou imunidade, e o caso ficou em segredo por quinze anos.
explicacao: Anthony Blunt dirigia o Instituto Courtauld de Arte, em Londres, e cuidava da coleção de pinturas da família real, primeiro como inspetor dos quadros do rei George VI, a partir de 1945, e depois da rainha. Seu livro de 1967 sobre o pintor Nicolas Poussin ainda é considerado um marco da história da arte. Ao mesmo tempo, era o "quarto homem" dos Cinco de Cambridge, um grupo de espiões formados naquela universidade que trabalharam para os soviéticos dos anos 1930 aos 1950. Seu auge como espião foi na Segunda Guerra, quando passou aos soviéticos informações sobre planos alemães que o governo britânico decidira não compartilhar. Em 1963, o MI5 soube da espionagem por um americano que ele recrutara. Em 1964, em troca de imunidade e de quinze anos de sigilo oficial, Blunt confessou. O secretário particular da rainha foi avisado logo depois. Sua vida mudou pouco. Em 1979, um livro descreveu o caso com pseudônimo, uma revista revelou que se tratava de Blunt, e a primeira-ministra Margaret Thatcher confirmou tudo no Parlamento. Ele perdeu o título de cavaleiro e morreu pouco mais de três anos depois.

fontes.trecho: was a leading British art historian and a Soviet spy. Blunt was a professor of the history of art at the University of London, the director of the Courtauld Institute of Art and Surveyor of the Queen's Pictures. His 1967 monograph on the French Baroque painter Nicolas Poussin is still widely regarded as a watershed book in art history. [...] He was the "fourth man" of the Cambridge Five, a group of Cambridge-educated spies who worked for the Soviets between the 1930s and the 1950s. [...] The height of Blunt's espionage activity was during the Second World War, when he passed intelligence to the Soviets  about Wehrmacht plans which the British government had decided to withhold. In 1964, after being offered immunity from prosecution, Blunt confessed to having been a spy for the Soviet Union. His confession was revealed by Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in November 1979. His knighthood was cancelled immediately and he died a little over three years later. [...] In April 1945, Blunt, who had worked part-time at the Royal Library, was offered and accepted the job of Surveyor of the King's Pictures. [...] In 1963, MI5 learned of Blunt's espionage from Straight, whom he had recruited. Blunt confessed to MI5 on 23 April 1964. The Private Secretary to the Sovereign was informed shortly thereafter, but Queen Elizabeth II herself was not officially informed until 1973. [...] In return for a full confession, the British government agreed to keep his espionage an official secret, though only for fifteen years, and granted him full immunity from prosecution. [...] Blunt's life was little affected by the knowledge of his treachery. [...] In 1979, Blunt's role was represented in Andrew Boyle's book Climate of Treason, in which Blunt was given the pseudonym "Maurice" [...] on 8 November Private Eye revealed that "Maurice" was Blunt. [...] In November 1979, Margaret Thatcher informed Parliament of Blunt's treachery and the immunity deal that had been arranged.

gancho: Para pedir resgate em Moscou, o agente duplo Oleg Gordievsky ficou numa esquina com uma sacola de supermercado britânico. Um agente do MI6 passou comendo um chocolate Mars: era a resposta. Ele fugiu num porta-malas.
explicacao: Gordievsky era oficial da KGB e passou informações ao serviço secreto britânico, o MI6, de 1974 a 1985. Entre outras coisas, mostrou o quanto a cúpula soviética temia um ataque nuclear da OTAN, a ponto de interpretar mal um exercício militar da OTAN. Em 1985, recém-promovido a chefe da KGB em Londres, foi chamado de volta a Moscou, drogado e interrogado. Não o prenderam, mas ficou sob vigilância. Para essa emergência, o MI6 tinha desde 1978 um plano de fuga, a Operação Pimlico, criado pela oficial Valerie Pettit. O sinal era combinado: num certo dia da semana, às 19h30, numa certa esquina, ele segurava uma sacola da rede Safeway; um agente britânico passava com uma sacola da Harrods, comendo um Mars, e os dois trocavam um olhar. Em 19 de julho, Gordievsky saiu para a corrida de sempre, despistou os vigias, pegou um trem para Leningrado e seguiu até perto da fronteira com a Finlândia. Ali, dois diplomatas britânicos e suas esposas o esconderam no porta-malas de um Ford Sierra. Na fronteira, uma das mulheres jogou no chão a fralda suja do bebê, e os cães farejadores se afastaram. Na URSS, ele foi condenado à morte à revelia.

fontes.trecho: Gordievsky was a double agent, providing information to the British Secret Intelligence Service (MI6) from 1974 to 1985. [...] The Soviet Union subsequently sentenced him to death in absentia. [...] The information supplied by Gordievsky provided the first proof of how worried the Soviet leadership had become about the possibility of a NATO nuclear first strike. [...] when the Soviets misinterpreted the NATO exercise Able Archer 83 as preparation for a first strike [...] In late April 1985, Gordievsky was promoted to KGB station chief (resident-designate or rezident) in London at the Soviet embassy. He was abruptly summoned back to Moscow by telegram on 16 May 1985. [...] he was taken to a KGB safe house outside Moscow, drugged, and interrogated. [...] After that, he was released and told that he would never work abroad again. [...] Under increasing surveillance and pressure in Moscow [...] An elaborate escape plan for extracting Gordievsky from the USSR had been devised by MI6 in 1978 [...] The escape plan was code-named "Operation Pimlico", and was devised by MI6 officer Valerie Pettit. [...] He waited on a particular street corner, on a particular weekday at 7:30 p.m., carrying a Safeway bag as a signal. An MI6 agent walked past carrying a Harrods bag, eating a Mars bar, and the two made eye contact. [...] On 19 July 1985, Gordievsky went for his usual jog. He managed to evade his KGB tails and boarded a train to Leningrad, and then travelled to a rendezvous south of Vyborg, near the Finnish border. [...] was smuggled across the border into Finland in the boot (trunk) of a Ford Sierra saloon. His couriers were two British diplomats and their wives, and to deter sniffer dogs at the Finnish border one of the wives dropped her baby's dirty nappy on the ground, causing the dogs to flee.

gancho: Em 1944, um ex-jogador de beisebol americano assistiu a uma palestra de Werner Heisenberg na Suíça com uma missão: se concluísse que os alemães estavam perto da bomba atômica, tinha ordens de matar o físico.
explicacao: Moe Berg jogou 15 temporadas nas grandes ligas de beisebol, quase sempre como apanhador, sem nunca passar de um jogador mediano. Era conhecido como o cérebro do beisebol: formado em Princeton, onde estudou sete línguas, entre elas latim, grego e sânscrito, e depois em direito em Columbia, lia vários jornais por dia. Numa excursão de astros do beisebol ao Japão, em 1934, subiu ao telhado de um hospital de Tóquio, um dos prédios mais altos da cidade, e filmou a cidade e o porto. Em 1942, entregou as imagens à inteligência americana, caso servissem para planejar bombardeios. Na guerra, entrou para o OSS, o serviço secreto americano da época, e passou 1944 rodando a Europa para entrevistar físicos e tentar convencer alguns a se mudarem para os EUA. Em dezembro, foi mandado à palestra de Heisenberg em Zurique para avaliar se algo que ele dissesse indicava uma bomba alemã próxima; nesse caso, devia atirar nele. Berg concluiu que os alemães não estavam perto. Depois da guerra, recusou a Medalha da Liberdade, a mais alta honraria para civis em tempo de guerra, sem dar explicação pública.

fontes.trecho: was an American professional baseball catcher and coach in Major League Baseball who later served as a spy for the Office of Strategic Services during World War II. He played 15 seasons in the major leagues, almost entirely for four American League teams, though he was never more than an average player and was better known for being "the brainiest guy in baseball." [...] Berg was a graduate of Princeton University and Columbia Law School, spoke several languages, and regularly read ten newspapers a day. [...] He studied seven languages: Latin, Greek, French, Spanish, Italian, German, and Sanskrit [...] Herb Hunter arranged for a group of All-Stars, including Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig [...] to tour Japan [...] On November 29, 1934, while the rest of the team was playing in Omiya [...] However, when Berg arrived he immediately went to the roof of the hospital, which was one of the tallest buildings in Tokyo, and filmed the city and port with his movie camera. In 1942, Berg provided American intelligence with his photos of the city in case they were of use to plan bombing raids. [...] From May to mid-December 1944, Berg hopped around Europe, interviewing physicists and trying to convince several to leave Europe and work in the United States. In November, news about Heisenberg giving a lecture in Zürich reached the OSS. Berg was assigned to attend the lecture, which took place on December 18, and determine "if anything Heisenberg said convinced him the Germans were close to a bomb." If Berg concluded that the Germans were close, he had orders to shoot Heisenberg; Berg determined that the Germans were not close. [...] Berg was awarded the Medal of Freedom, the highest honor given to civilians during wartime, from President Harry S. Truman for his service. He declined to accept it without any public explanation.

gancho: Antes de virar ícone da cozinha francesa, Julia Child trabalhou no serviço secreto americano, perto de cientistas que criavam uma "receita" de repelente de tubarão. Na época, ela se dizia um desastre na cozinha.
explicacao: Com 1,88 m de altura, Julia McWilliams era alta demais para os corpos femininos do Exército e da Marinha dos EUA. Em 1942, entrou para o OSS, o serviço secreto criado naquele ano e antecessor da CIA, onde começou como datilógrafa. Em 1943, passou um ano como assistente executiva do cientista Harold Coolidge, que chefiava uma divisão de equipamentos de resgate. Um dos projetos era um repelente de tubarão, pedido pelo comando militar para levantar o moral de marinheiros e aviadores que caíam em águas infestadas. Os pesquisadores testaram mais de 100 substâncias; entre as mais promissoras estavam extratos de carne de tubarão podre e sais de cobre. A vencedora foi o acetato de cobre, misturado a um corante preto num tablete que, na água, cheirava a tubarão morto. A Marinha duvidava que aquilo segurasse um ataque de verdade, mas distribuiu o "Shark Chaser" até os anos 1970. O tamanho do papel dela é incerto: há relatos de que ela mesma cozinhava misturas de teste, mas a CIA diz apenas que ela trabalhava perto dos oficiais que criaram a fórmula, embora Julia falasse no repelente "que desenvolvemos". Mais tarde, servindo no Ceilão, ela conheceu no próprio OSS o futuro marido, Paul Child, que a apresentou à alta gastronomia.

fontes.titulo: Julia Child and the OSS Recipe for Shark Repellent (CIA)
fontes.trecho: To boost morale, the Joint Chiefs of Staff requested the Office of Strategic Services (OSS, CIA's predecessor) to lead the hunt to find a shark repellent. [...] raising alarm amongst sailors and airmen who increasingly found themselves conducting dangerous missions over shark-infested waters. [...] Julia McWilliams (better known by her married name, Julia Child) joined the newly-created OSS in 1942 in search of adventure. [...] In fact, at this time, Julia was self-admittedly a disaster in the kitchen. Perhaps all the more fitting that she soon found herself working in close proximity to OSS officers who developed a recipe that even a shark would refuse to eat. [...] the ERE Special Projects division was headed by Captain Harold J. Coolidge [...] Julia Child worked for Coolidge for a year in 1943 as an Executive Assistant. [...] After trying over 100 different substances—including common poisons—the researchers found several promising possibilities: extracts from decayed shark meat, organic acids, and several copper salts [...] the most effective repellent was copper acetate. [...] copper acetate was mixed with black dye, which was then formed into a little disk-shaped "cake" that smelled like a dead shark when released into the water. [...] Despite the promising results of initial field tests, the Navy remained skeptical. [...] it was the Bureau's opinion "that it is illogical to expect that such effect as was shown in normal feeding behavior would give any promise of affecting the voracious behavior of the few species known to have attacked man." [...] The Navy did end up issuing the shark repellent based on the original OSS recipe—also known as "Shark Chaser"—until the 1970s [...] I understand the shark repellent we developed is being used today for downed space equipment

Child joined the Office of Strategic Services (OSS) in 1942 after finding that at 6 feet 2 inches (1.88 m), she was too tall to enlist in the Women's Army Corps (WACs) or in the U.S. Navy's WAVES. She began her OSS career as a typist at its headquarters in Washington, D.C. [...] "Child's solution was to experiment with cooking various concoctions as a shark repellent," [...] Child was posted to Kandy, Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) [...] While she was in Kandy, she met Paul Cushing Child, who was also an OSS employee. [...] Paul [...] was known for his sophisticated palate and had introduced his wife to fine cuisine.

gancho: Richard Sorge espionou para a URSS no Japão fingindo ser jornalista nazista. Virou confidente do embaixador alemão e avisou Moscou da invasão de 1941, mas Stalin ignorou. Já a data exata, ele provavelmente nunca deu.
explicacao: Alemão a serviço da inteligência militar soviética, Sorge recebeu ordens de entrar no Partido Nazista e de se afastar de qualquer militante de esquerda. Encarnou tão bem o papel de nazista convicto que, quando partiu para o Japão, em 1933, o ministro da propaganda Joseph Goebbels foi ao seu jantar de despedida. Em Tóquio, como correspondente do Frankfurter Zeitung, o jornal mais prestigiado da Alemanha, tornou-se amigo do adido militar Eugen Ott. Quando Ott virou embaixador, em 1938, os dois tomavam café da manhã juntos todos os dias, e Sorge às vezes redigia os telegramas que Ott mandava a Berlim. Em 30 de maio de 1941, avisou Moscou de que o ataque alemão viria na segunda metade de junho. Stalin ignorou esse e outros alertas. Diz a lenda que ele cravou o dia, 22 de junho. O historiador Gordon Prange não aceitou essa versão: concluiu, em 1984, que o mais perto que Sorge chegou foi 20 de junho, e que o próprio espião nunca disse ter sabido a data certa. Ele avisou também que o Japão não atacaria a URSS, informação que, para alguns autores, ajudou a liberar tropas do Extremo Oriente para defender Moscou, embora Moscou já soubesse disso pela quebra de códigos japoneses. Preso em 1941 e enforcado em 1944, Sorge foi declarado Herói da União Soviética em 1964.

fontes.trecho: was a German journalist and Soviet military intelligence officer who was active before and during World War II and worked undercover as a German journalist in both Nazi Germany and the Empire of Japan. [...] He was posthumously awarded the title of Hero of the Soviet Union in 1964. [...] He was instructed to join the Nazi Party and not to associate with any left-wing activists. [...] Sorge was so successful at establishing his cover as an intensely Nazi journalist that when he departed Germany, Joseph Goebbels attended his farewell dinner. [...] Sorge arrived in Yokohama on 6 September 1933. After landing in Japan, Sorge became the Japan correspondent for the Frankfurter Zeitung. As it was the most prestigious newspaper in Germany [...] After Ott became the ambassador to Japan in April 1938, Sorge had breakfast with him daily and they discussed German–Japanese relations in detail, and Sorge sometimes drafted the cables that Ott sent under his name to Berlin. [...] On 30 May 1941, Sorge reported to Moscow, "Berlin informed Ott that German attack will commence in the latter part of June. [...] Moscow received the reports, but Stalin and other top Soviet leaders ultimately ignored Sorge's warnings, as well as those of other sources [...] It has been rumoured that Sorge provided the exact date of "Barbarossa", but the historian Gordon Prange in 1984 concluded that the closest Sorge came was 20 June and that Sorge himself never claimed to have discovered the correct date (22 June) in advance. [...] Various writers have speculated that the information allowed the release of Siberian divisions for the Battle of Moscow [...] However, Sorge was not the only source of Soviet intelligence about Japan, as Soviet codebreakers had broken the Japanese diplomatic codes and so Moscow knew from signals intelligence that there would be no Japanese attack on the Soviet Union in 1941. [...] Sorge's penultimate message to Moscow in October 1941 reported, "The Soviet Far East can be considered safe from Japanese attack". [...] Meanwhile, Sorge befriended General Eugen Ott, the German military attaché to Japan [...] Sorge was arrested shortly thereafter, on 18 October 1941, in Tokyo. [...] Sorge was hanged on 7 November 1944

gancho: Antes da Companhia Holandesa das Índias Orientais, de 1602, sócios de viagens às Índias recebiam a sua parte na volta da frota. Na VOC, o capital ficava preso: quem quisesse sair tinha de vender as ações a outro.
explicacao: Era costume, na época, financiar uma empresa só pelo tempo de uma viagem e liquidá-la quando a frota voltava. A VOC, criada em 1602 pelos Estados Gerais holandeses, mudou a regra: o capital seria permanente enquanto a companhia existisse, e a responsabilidade dos sócios ficava limitada ao que tinham investido. Qualquer cidadão da República Holandesa podia comprar ações, e elas passaram a trocar de mãos em mercados ao ar livre, um dos quais virou a Bolsa de Amsterdã. A companhia tinha poderes quase de Estado: podia fazer guerra, assinar tratados, cunhar moedas e fundar colônias. Em 1669, mantinha mais de 150 navios mercantes, 40 de guerra e um exército particular de 10 mil soldados. Os acionistas também estrearam conflitos que hoje parecem modernos. Em 1609, Isaac Le Maire, um dos maiores investidores, entrou com uma petição contra a diretoria, considerada o primeiro registro de ativismo de acionistas. Em 1622, investidores revoltados reclamaram que os livros contábeis tinham sido "lambuzados de toucinho" para que os cães os comessem, e exigiram uma auditoria. A VOC faliu e foi dissolvida em 1799. Na Holanda, a sigla ganhou um apelido amargo: "vergaan onder corruptie", "pereceu sob a corrupção".

fontes.trecho: one of the first joint-stock companies in the world. Established on 20 March 1602 by the States General of the Netherlands amalgamating existing companies [...] Shares in the company could be purchased by any citizen of the Dutch Republic and bought and sold in open-air secondary markets, one of which became the Amsterdam Stock Exchange. The company possessed quasi-governmental powers, including the ability to wage war, imprison and execute convicts, negotiate treaties, strike its own coins, and establish colonies. [...] At the time, it was customary for a company to be funded only for the duration of a single voyage and to be liquidated upon the return of the fleet. [...] The VOC therefore was a limited liability company. Also, the capital would be permanent during the lifetime of the company. As a consequence, investors that wished to liquidate their interest in the interim could only do this by selling their share to others on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange. [...] By 1669, the VOC was the richest private company the world had ever seen, with over 150 merchant ships, 40 warships, 50,000 employees, a private army of 10,000 soldiers [...] In 1622, the history's first recorded shareholder revolt also happened among the VOC investors who complained that the company account books had been "smeared with bacon" so that they might be "eaten by dogs". The investors demanded a "reeckeninge", a proper financial audit. [...] On 24 January 1609, Le Maire filed a petition against the VOC, marking the first recorded expression of shareholder activism. [...] Initially the largest single shareholder in the VOC [...] the phrase perished under corruption (vergaan onder corruptie, also abbreviated VOC in Dutch) came to summarise the company's future. [...] the company went bankrupt and was formally dissolved in 1799.

gancho: No auge, a Companhia Britânica das Índias Orientais, uma empresa com acionistas, tinha cerca de 260 mil soldados, em certas épocas o dobro do exército britânico. De um prédio em Londres, governava boa parte da Índia.
explicacao: A companhia nasceu no último dia de 1600, quando a rainha atendeu ao pedido de um grupo de comerciantes, para negociar no oceano Índico. O passo decisivo para virar potência territorial foi a Batalha de Plassey, em 1757: a força de Robert Clive, com cerca de 800 soldados e 2.200 sipaios, derrotou o nababo de Bengala, mas venceu sobretudo graças a uma conspiração prévia com o comandante do inimigo, Mir Jafar, que virou o novo nababo. Em 1765, o imperador mogol deu à companhia a diwani, o direito de arrecadar e administrar os impostos de Bengala, Bihar e Orissa. Uma empresa privada, com três exércitos próprios, passou a cobrar impostos. O governo da companhia é acusado de ter empobrecido boa parte da população e de ter conduzido mal a grande fome de Bengala, em 1770. O fim veio depois da rebelião indiana de 1857: em 1858, a Coroa assumiu o governo, as tropas e a administração. A companhia ainda sobreviveu como uma sombra, cuidando do comércio de chá para o governo, até ser formalmente dissolvida em 1874.

fontes.trecho: The East India Company (EIC) was an English, and later British, joint-stock company that was founded in 1600 and dissolved in 1874. It was formed for Indian Ocean trade [...] At its peak, the company was the largest corporation in the world by various measures and had its own armed forces in the form of the company's three presidency armies, totalling about 260,000 soldiers, twice the size of the British Army at certain times. [...] the company used torture to extract taxes, reduced much of the population to poverty and mishandled the Great Bengal famine of 1770 [...] Following the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the Government of India Act 1858 led to the British Crown assuming direct control [...] They convened again a year later, on 31 December 1600, and this time they succeeded; the Queen responded favourably [...] The battle took place on 23 June 1757, when Robert Clive's force of roughly 800 soldiers and 2,200 sepoys defeated the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daula. The company was victorious largely through a prior conspiracy with the Nawab’s commander, Mir Jafar, instead of through force. The victory installed Mir Jafar as the Nawab [...] culminating in 1765 when the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II granted it the diwani, the right to collect and administer the revenues of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. [...] The British government took over its Indian possessions, its administrative powers and machinery, and its armed forces. [...] The company remained in existence in vestigial form, continuing to manage the tea trade on behalf of the British Government [...] The company's headquarters in London, from which much of India was governed, was East India House in Leadenhall Street.

gancho: Um funcionário de uma companhia de navegação de Liverpool percebeu o trabalho forçado no Congo de Leopoldo II pelas cargas: os navios voltavam com borracha e marfim e iam com armas, correntes e explosivos.
explicacao: De 1885 a 1908, o Estado Livre do Congo foi propriedade particular do rei Leopoldo II, e não parte da Bélgica. O rei o governava de Bruxelas e nunca pisou lá. Edmund Dene Morel trabalhava desde 1891 na Elder Dempster, que fazia a linha entre Antuérpia e o porto congolês de Boma. Por falar francês, ia com frequência à Bélgica e via as contas internas. Os navios que partiam para o Congo carregavam armas, correntes, munição, explosivos e artigos sem relação com o comércio, enquanto os que voltavam vinham cheios de borracha e marfim. Morel concluiu que aquela riqueza era arrancada à força dos congoleses. Segundo o historiador Adam Hochschild, ele estava certo: o que saía do Congo valia cinco vezes o que entrava. Denúncias já circulavam havia uma década, desde o americano George Washington Williams, mas faltavam números; Morel trouxe os dados do comércio. A empresa lhe ofereceu promoção e depois um cargo sem trabalho em troca de silêncio, e ele recusou, saindo em 1901 para virar jornalista. Com o cônsul Roger Casement, criou a Associação para a Reforma do Congo, apoiada por Arthur Conan Doyle e Mark Twain. As fotografias da missionária Alice Seeley Harris reforçaram a campanha: só nos Estados Unidos, em 1906, foram projetadas em 200 reuniões em 49 cidades. Em 1908, sob pressão internacional, o parlamento belga anexou o território.

fontes.trecho: As a young official at the shipping company Elder Dempster, Morel observed a fortune being made in the import of Congo rubber and the shipping out of guns and manacles. He correctly deduced that the rubber and other resources were being extracted from the Congolese by force [...] founded the Congo Reform Association and published the West African Mail. With the help of celebrities such as Arthur Conan Doyle and Mark Twain [...] In 1891, Morel obtained a clerkship with Elder Dempster, a Liverpool shipping firm. [...] Elder Dempster had a shipping contract with the Congo Free State for the connection between Antwerp and Boma. Due to his knowledge of French, Morel was often sent to Belgium, where he was able to view the internal accounts of the Congo Free State held by Elder Dempster. The knowledge that the Elder Dempster ships leaving Belgium for the Congo regularly carried guns, chains, ordnance and explosives, and articles which were remote from trade purposes, while ships arriving from the colony came back full of valuable products such as raw rubber and ivory [...] According to author Adam Hochschild, Morel's conclusions were correct—the value of the goods coming from the Congo Free State was five times that of the goods coming from Europe [...] The company soon offered Morel an overseas promotion and then a sinecure consultancy in return for a guarantee of his silence. Morel refused both offers, and left the company in 1901 to become a full-time journalist. [...] Casement convinced Morel to establish an organisation for dealing specifically with the Congo question, the Congo Reform Association [...] In 1900, Morel put new life into the campaign against Congo misrule (begun a decade before by the American George Washington Williams) with a series of articles detailing his discoveries about the Congo Free State trade imbalances.

a state and absolute monarchy in Central Africa from 1885 to 1908. It was privately owned by King Leopold II [...] The Congo Free State was not a part of, nor did it belong to, Belgium. [...] The Free State was privately controlled by Leopold from Brussels; he never visited it. The state included the entire area of the present Democratic Republic of the Congo and existed from 1885 to 1908, when the Belgian Parliament reluctantly annexed the state as a colony belonging to Belgium after international pressure.

Her photography helped to expose the human rights abuses in the Congo Free State under the regime of King Leopold II of the Belgians. [...] In early 1906, they toured the United States. John wrote that they had presented her images at 200 meetings in 49 cities via magic lantern screenings.

gancho: Hong Kong não foi toda arrendada por 99 anos: a ilha e a península de Kowloon foram cedidas aos britânicos "para sempre". Só os Novos Territórios eram arrendados, mas o fim desse prazo decidiu o destino de tudo.
explicacao: A ilha de Hong Kong passou ao Reino Unido "em perpetuidade" pelo Tratado de Nanquim, de 1842, depois da Primeira Guerra do Ópio. Em 1860, depois da Segunda, foi a vez da península de Kowloon, também para sempre. O arrendamento só veio em 1898: com a França arrendando um porto a cerca de 340 km dali, os britânicos obtiveram da dinastia Qing, de graça e por 99 anos, os Novos Territórios e 235 ilhas. Pela lei britânica da época, 99 anos era o prazo máximo de um arrendamento de terras, e o negociador britânico achava que um prazo tão longo indicava, na prática, uma cessão permanente. Não foi. Em meados dos anos 1970, investidores começaram a se preocupar, porque o governo colonial não podia conceder lotes nos Novos Territórios além de 1997. Em 1979, o governador Murray MacLehose levou o problema a Deng Xiaoping, e a conversa evoluiu até a Declaração Conjunta, assinada em 1984. Margaret Thatcher disse depois que, se o Reino Unido tentasse ficar com a ilha, a China nem precisaria invadir: bastaria cortar o fornecimento de água. Pelo acordo, Hong Kong manteria seu sistema por 50 anos, sob o lema "um país, dois sistemas".

fontes.titulo: Convention for the Extension of Hong Kong Territory
fontes.trecho: leasing to the United Kingdom for 99 years, at no charge, the New Territories (as the area became known) and New Kowloon, including 235 islands. [...] In the Treaty of Nanking, in 1842, the Qing government agreed to make Hong Kong a Crown colony, ceding it 'in perpetuity', following the British victory in the First Opium War. [...] Under British law at the time, a 99-year lease was the maximum allowed for the lease of land.

first in 1860 with the addition of Kowloon Peninsula and Stonecutters Island, as both were ceded in perpetuity, and again in 1898 when Britain obtained a 99-year lease for the New Territories. The date of the handover in 1997 marked the end of this lease. [...] When France obtained a lease for Guangzhouwan, only 210 miles (340 km) away from Hong Kong, Britain entered into negotiations with the Qing to acquire the New Territories as a compensatory concession in 1898. The British negotiator considered the 99-year lease term to be sufficiently suggestive that the ceded area would be a permanent cession, which was granted rent-free. [...] Local investors began expressing their concern in the mid-1970s over the long-term viability of continued real estate investment. The colonial government could not legally grant new land leases in the New Territories past 1997 and needed to resolve the uncertainty with the Chinese government. [...] hatcher later pointed out in 1997 that if Britain had tried to retain Hong Kong Island, the Chinese did not have to militarily invade as they could have simply just turned off the supply of water [...] the principle of "one country, two systems". [...] remain unchanged for a period of 50 years after 1997. [...] The Sino-British Joint Declaration was a treaty signed in 1984 between the governments of China and the United Kingdom which set the conditions in which Hong Kong was transferred to Chinese control [...] During an official visit to Beijing in March 1979, Governor Murray MacLehose raised the issue with Vice Premier Deng Xiaoping.

gancho: A Conferência de Berlim (1884–1885) é lembrada como a reunião em que europeus retalharam a África, sem africanos. Mas, segundo um estudo de 2024, as únicas fronteiras fixadas ali foram as da região do Congo.
explicacao: Bismarck convidou 13 nações europeias e os Estados Unidos para combinar uma política comum para o continente. Nenhum país africano foi chamado. O sultão Barghash, de Zanzibar, foi o único chefe de Estado africano a pedir para mandar um representante, e o pedido foi recusado, por pressão de uma organização antiescravagista britânica, já que Zanzibar participava do tráfico de escravizados. A conferência reconheceu a associação controlada pessoalmente pelo rei Leopoldo II no Congo e fixou o princípio da ocupação efetiva: para ter reconhecida uma posse no litoral africano, a potência precisava notificar as demais e mostrar presença ali. Na versão final, bastava uma base costeira, sem controle real do interior. A conferência ajudou a abrir um período de colonização mais intensa. Mas a imagem de diplomatas desenhando o mapa do continente numa mesa é exagerada, segundo parte dos historiadores. O estudo de 2024 concluiu que as fronteiras do Congo, depois revistas, foram as únicas definidas na conferência, e que a maioria das fronteiras africanas só tomou a forma final mais de duas décadas depois, em acordos bilaterais. Em 1885, o jornal Lagos Observer, da atual Nigéria, chamou a conferência de roubo em larga escala. Em 1914, 90% das terras africanas estavam sob controle europeu, e só a Etiópia e a Libéria seguiam independentes.

fontes.trecho: Otto von Bismarck, the Chancellor of Germany, called on representatives of 13 European nations, as well as the United States, to take part in the Berlin Conference in 1884 to work out a joint policy on the African continent. No African countries were invited to the congress, but Sultan Barghash Bin Seyyid of Zanzibar had requested to send a representative to the conference, the only African head of state to do so, which was rejected due to pressure by the Anti-Slavery reporter, an organization in Britain which had pressured the government to reject the participation of Zanzibar at the conference due to its activity in the slave t [...] The conference contributed to ushering in a period of heightened colonial activity by European powers, and is sometimes cited as being responsible for the "carve-up of Africa." However, some scholars warn against overstating its role in the colonial partitioning of Africa, drawing attention to the many bilateral agreements concluded before and after the conference. A 2024 study found that the only borders set at the conference were those of the Congo region (which were subsequently revised), and that most of Africa's borders did not take their final form until over two decades later. [...] the codification of the Principle of Effective Occupation (see below), which mandated that "authority had to be established throughout the respective territory" in order for a colonial claim to be legitimised. [...] One 1885 entry of a Nigerian newspaper, the Lagos Observer, described the Conference as a "robbery on so large a scale" [...] By 1914, 90% of all the land that makes up Africa was under European control. [...] By 1914, the only modern nations on the continent of Africa that remained independent were Ethiopia and Liberia. [...] agreed on a common framework for the recognition of European ''effective occupation'' of African coastal territory [...] any power attempting to take possession of or assume a protectorate over any territory within the African continent would be required to notify the other signatory powers before the possession or colony could be officially recognised. [...] the powers ultimately agreed that effective occupation could be established by a European state setting up a coastal base, from which it could expand into the interior. The conference participants did not view the rules of occupation as requiring full European hegemony on the ground.

The conference officially recognized the International Congo Association, and specified that it should have no connection with Belgium, beyond a personal union, or any other country, but would be under the personal control of King Leopold.

gancho: No século XVI, ninguém conseguia determinar longitudes com precisão. Portugal e Espanha disputaram as Ilhas das Especiarias, cada um com mapas que as punham na sua metade do mundo. No fim, Portugal pagou 350 mil ducados.
explicacao: O Tratado de Tordesilhas, de 1494, dividiu o mundo entre as duas coroas por uma linha no Atlântico. O problema surgiu do outro lado do planeta: em 1521, a frota de Fernão de Magalhães, já sob o comando de Elcano, chegou às Molucas pelo leste, e os dois reinos as reivindicaram. Em 1524, cada coroa nomeou três astrônomos e cartógrafos, três pilotos e três matemáticos para localizar a linha oposta à de Tordesilhas. Segundo o cronista Pedro Mártir de Anghiera, um menino parou a delegação portuguesa, perguntou se ela ia mesmo dividir o mundo e, diante do sim, baixou as calças e sugeriu que a linha passasse pelo seu traseiro. As reuniões, em Badajoz e Elvas, não deram em nada: o conhecimento geográfico não permitia fixar longitudes, e cada lado escolheu mapas e globos que lhe davam razão. O impasse acabou com o Tratado de Saragoça, de 1529. A linha passou a ficar 297 léguas e meia a leste das ilhas, deixando-as com Portugal, que em troca pagou 350 mil ducados de ouro ao imperador Carlos V. Uma cláusula permitia desfazer o negócio devolvendo o dinheiro, mas o imperador precisava dele para guerrear contra a França.

fontes.trecho: signed on 22 April 1529 by King John III of Portugal and the Habsburg Emperor Charles V in the Aragonese city of Zaragoza. [...] because both kingdoms claimed the lucrative Spice Islands (now Indonesia's Malukus) for themselves, asserting that they were within their area of influence as specified in 1494 by the Treaty of Tordesillas. [...] On 6 November 1521, the Moluccas—"the cradle of all spices"—were reached from the east by Magellan's fleet, now under Juan Sebastián Elcano. [...] In 1524, both kingdoms organised the "Junta de Badajoz–Elvas" to resolve the dispute. Each crown appointed three astronomers and cartographers, three pilots and three mathematicians, who formed a committee to establish the exact location of the antimeridian of Tordesillas [...] According to contemporary Castilian writer Peter Martyr d'Anghiera, a small boy stopped the Portuguese delegation and asked if they intended to divide up the world. The delegation answered that they were. The boy responded by baring his backside and suggesting that they draw their line through his intergluteal cleft. The board met several times, at Badajoz and Elvas, without reaching an agreement. Geographic knowledge at that time was inadequate for an accurate assignment of longitude, and each group chose maps or globes that showed the islands to be in their own hemisphere. [...] The Treaty of Zaragoza laid down that the eastern border between the two domain zones was 297+1⁄2 leagues [...] This left the islands within the Portuguese domain. In exchange, the King of Portugal paid Emperor Charles V 350,000 gold ducats. The treaty included a safeguard clause which stated that the deal would be undone if at any time the emperor wished to revoke it, with the Portuguese being reimbursed the money [...] That never happened, however, because the emperor desperately needed the Portuguese money to finance the War of the League of Cognac against his archrival Francis I of France.

gancho: Um verbo levou à guerra: no tratado de 1889 entre Etiópia e Itália, a versão em amárico dizia que o imperador "podia" usar a Itália nas relações exteriores; a italiana, que "devia". A Itália perdeu a guerra em Adwa.
explicacao: O Tratado de Wuchale foi assinado em maio de 1889 por Menelik II e pelo conde Pietro Antonelli, com vinte artigos em duas línguas. Um dos artigos dizia que as duas versões teriam o mesmo conteúdo, mas o artigo 17 não tinha. No texto em amárico, o imperador podia, se quisesse, tratar com outras potências por meio do governo italiano. No italiano, era obrigado a isso, o que na prática fazia da Etiópia um protetorado. Segundo os italianos, foi um erro na tradução de um verbo. Em outubro de 1889, a Itália avisou os governos europeus de que a Etiópia era seu protetorado, e quase todos aceitaram; as exceções foram o Império Otomano e a Rússia, que não queria ver um país ortodoxo submetido a um católico. Menelik denunciou o tratado, e a Itália invadiu em 1895. Em 1º de março de 1896, em Adwa, um exército etíope estimado entre 73 mil e mais de 100 mil homens, em grande parte armado com fuzis modernos comprados da França e da Rússia, derrotou a força italiana. A Itália teve de reconhecer a soberania etíope, o governo de Francesco Crispi caiu, e a vitória virou símbolo para os movimentos de descolonização e o pan-africanismo. Hoje, o Dia da Vitória de Adwa é feriado na Etiópia.

fontes.trecho: The signing parties were King Menelik II of Shewa, acting as Emperor of Ethiopia, and Count Pietro Antonelli representing Italy, on 2 May 1889 [...] The treaty has twenty articles written in two languages, Amharic and Italian; however, there were marked differences in the Italian and the Amharic versions of the treaty [...] Article 17 was written differently in the Ethiopian and Italian versions of the treaty [...] Article 19 said that the treaty would be written in both languages and both versions would present the same information. [...] The misunderstanding, according to the Italians, was due to the mistranslation of a verb, which formed a permissive clause in  Amharic and a mandatory one in  Italian. [...] According to this version, the Emperor of Ethiopia was granted a choice and was not mandated to use the Italian government to conduct foreign relations [...] On the other hand, the Italian version stated that Ethiopia was obliged to conduct all foreign affairs through Italian authorities, in effect making Ethiopia an Italian protectorate. [...] However, in October 1889, the Italians informed all other European governments that Ethiopia was now an Italian protectorate [...] With the exceptions of the Ottoman Empire, which still maintained its claim to Eritrea, and Russia, which disliked the idea of an Orthodox nation being subjugated to a Roman Catholic nation, all of the European powers accepted the Italian claim to a protectorate. [...] the treaty was eventually denounced by Menelik II in 1894 and the Italians invaded Ethiopia in 1895.

It was fought on 1 March 1896, near the town of Adwa between the Ethiopian Empire under Emperor Menelik II and an Italian colonial force [...] Emperor Menelik II mobilized a massive army, with estimates ranging from 73,000 to over 100,000 men, mostly equipped with modern rifles imported from France and Russia. [...] The defeat forced Italy to recognize Ethiopia's sovereignty in the Treaty of Addis Ababa. Adwa resulted in the fall of the government of Francesco Crispi [...] became rallying points for later African nationalists during their struggle for decolonization, as well as activists and leaders of the Pan-African movement. [...] The Adwa Victory Day is a public holiday

gancho: Depois da Revolução dos Cravos, em 1974, Portugal se dispôs a devolver Macau à China de imediato. A China recusou. Macau só foi entregue em 1999, fechando quase seis séculos de império colonial português.
explicacao: O império português foi o primeiro e o mais duradouro dos impérios coloniais europeus. O marco inicial costuma ser a tomada de Ceuta, no norte da África, em 1415, que decepcionou: as caravanas do Saara simplesmente mudaram de rota e evitaram a cidade. Macau, por sua vez, foi ocupada por mercadores portugueses em 1557, e um tratado de 1887 deu a Portugal direitos perpétuos sobre ela. Depois do golpe de 25 de abril de 1974, o novo governo, comprometido com a descolonização, propôs entregar Macau logo. Pequim não quis, por temer o efeito sobre Hong Kong. Em 1975, Portugal retirou as últimas tropas, e em 1976 os dois países passaram a chamar Macau de "território chinês sob supervisão portuguesa". Nas negociações de 1987, os portugueses voltaram a oferecer a devolução, e os chineses rejeitaram aquela data, como já tinham rejeitado pedidos em 1967, 1975 e 1977. A China propôs 1997, como Hong Kong, e Portugal não aceitou; Portugal sugeriu 2004 ou 2007, e a China quis antes de 2000. Acertaram 1999. Na meia-noite de 20 de dezembro daquele ano, terminaram 442 anos de domínio português em Macau.

fontes.trecho: The handover of Macau from the Portuguese Republic to the People's Republic of China (PRC) officially occurred at midnight on 20 December 1999. This event ended 442 years of Portuguese rule in the former settlement, which began in 1557. Macau was settled by Portuguese merchants that year [...] signed the 1887 Sino-Portuguese Treaty of Peking that gave Portugal perpetual colonial rights to Macau [...] On 25 April 1974, a group of left-wing Portuguese officers organised a coup d'état in Lisbon [...] The new government began to transition Portugal into a liberal democracy that was committed to decolonization. The new government carried out such policies, and initially proposed Macau's handover to China at once. However, the Chinese government rejected proposals for an early handover, believing that it would impact relations with Hong Kong. Nevertheless, on 31 December 1975, the Portuguese government had already withdrawn its remaining troops from Macau. In 1976, both Portugal and the PRC recognised Macau as a "Chinese territory under Portuguese supervision". [...] The handover marked the end of almost six centuries of the Portuguese Empire since 1415. [...] During the negotiations, Portuguese representatives again offered to return Macau in 1987, but Chinese representatives rejected that year (as well rejecting previous requests in 1967, 1975, and 1977). China requested 1997, the same year as Hong Kong, but Portugal refused. 2004 was suggested by Portugal, as well as 2007 [...] However, China insisted for a year before 2000 [...] Eventually, the year 1999 was agreed upon.

The Portuguese Empire was the first and longest lasting of the European colonial empires. [...] In 1415 an attack was made on Ceuta [...] The Portuguese were unable to use it as a base for further expansion into the hinterland, and the trans-Saharan caravans merely shifted their routes to bypass Ceuta and/or used alternative Muslim ports. [...] Although Ceuta proved to be a disappointment for the Portuguese

gancho: Depois de denunciar os campos de concentração britânicos na Guerra dos Bôeres, a inglesa Emily Hobhouse foi impedida de desembarcar na África do Sul. Hoje, suas cinzas estão lá, num monumento, e ela é vista como heroína.
explicacao: Na fase final da guerra, dominada pela remoção de civis, os britânicos destruíram fazendas, plantações e rebanhos dos bôeres, descendentes de colonos holandeses, para que os guerrilheiros não tivessem onde se abastecer. Dezenas de milhares de civis foram levados para campos: 45 para bôeres, quase todos mulheres e crianças, e 64 para africanos negros. Hobhouse, ativista inglesa de causas sociais, criou um fundo de ajuda e chegou à Colônia do Cabo no fim de 1900. Convenceu as autoridades a deixá-la visitar campos e, de volta à Inglaterra, publicou em 1901 um relatório de 40 páginas sobre superlotação, doenças e falta de comida. Foi atacada pelo governo e pela imprensa, mas uma comissão oficial, chefiada por Millicent Fawcett, confirmou o que ela descrevera, sem lhe dar crédito. Em outubro de 1901, ao voltar à Cidade do Cabo, ela não teve permissão para desembarcar e foi deportada cinco dias depois. Mais de 100 mil sul-africanos negros também ficaram presos em campos, em condições piores, e isso quase não causou indignação na época. Hobhouse morreu em 1926, e suas cinzas foram postas no Monumento Nacional das Mulheres, em Bloemfontein, onde era vista como heroína.

fontes.trecho: was a British welfare campaigner, anti-war activist, and pacifist. She is primarily remembered for bringing to the attention of the British public, and working to change, the deprived conditions inside the British concentration camps in South Africa [...] She set up the South African Women and Children Distress Fund and sailed for the Cape Colony on 7 December 1900 to supervise its distribution, arriving on 27 December. [...] Hobhouse had persuaded the authorities to let her visit several British concentration camps and to deliver her 40-page report on conditions at the camps [...] As a result, a formal commission was set up and a team of official investigators headed by Millicent Fawcett was sent to inspect the camps. Overcrowding in bad, unhygienic conditions due to bad planning, poor rations, diseases, and exposure to the elements [...] When Hobhouse returned to England, she received criticism and hostility from the British government and the press. [...] hich corroborated her account of the shocking conditions. However, Hobhouse was never acknowledged for her contribution in their report. Hobhouse returned to Cape Town in October 1901, but was not permitted to land, and was deported five days after arriving. [...] Hobhouse died in Kensington on 9 June 1926. Her ashes were put in a niche in the National Women's Monument at Bloemfontein, where she was regarded as a heroine.

More than 100,000 Black South Africans—many of whom opposed the Boers in their war—were held in camps in worse conditions, but their treatment elicited little outrage. [...] The British destroyed Boer farms under their scorched-earth policy, including the systematic destruction of crops, the slaughtering or removal of livestock, and the burning of homesteads and farms in order to prevent the Boers from resupplying themselves from a home base. As this happened, tens of thousands of men, women, and children were forcibly moved into camps. Eventually, authorities built a total of 45 tented camps for Boer internees and 64 additional camps for Black Africans. The vast majority of Boers who remained in the local camps were women and children. [...] Historian Thomas Pakenham describes the last phases of the war as being dominated by "the clearance of civilians—uprooting a whole nation".
Orange Free State, a Boer republic founded by Dutch settlers.

gancho: Para cobrar o imposto do sal, os britânicos mantiveram na Índia uma barreira alfandegária de mais de 4 mil km, com longos trechos de sebe viva de espinhos. Foi esquecida, até um conservador de biblioteca ir atrás dela.
explicacao: O imposto do sal pesava: em Bengala, o governador-geral da Companhia das Índias Orientais o multiplicou mais de dez vezes até 1788, e uma família comum pagava por ano o equivalente a uns dois meses de salário de um trabalhador. O maior risco para a arrecadação era o sal contrabandeado de Estados fora do domínio britânico direto. A partir de 1803, surgiram postos alfandegários que viraram uma linha contínua, batizada em 1843. Em 1869, o governo mandou ligá-la de ponta a ponta, do Himalaia até perto da baía de Bengala, numa distância comparada à de Londres a Constantinopla. Os espinhos secos usados como cerca provavelmente criaram raízes, e o comissário Allan Octavian Hume testou arbustos espinhosos nativos para formar uma sebe viva, com pelo menos 2,4 m de altura e, em alguns trechos, 3,7 m.
